say.text: A ventilated patient with acute cholecystitis needs a TG18 organ check. Which single blood gas result meets a Grade III respiratory criterion?

choices.label: PaO2 below 60 mmHg on room air
Arterial pH below 7.30 with a raised lactate
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: That is not the right choice.
A PaO2 of 60 is the everyday cut-off for respiratory failure in general medicine; TG18 scores the lungs on its own measure.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check this one: the everyday oxygen and acidosis numbers are the swap to avoid, because TG18 has its own organ thresholds.

say.text: That is not the right choice.
A pH of 7.30 is an acidosis threshold from critical-care practice, and TG18 does not grade the lungs by pH.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check this one: the everyday oxygen and acidosis numbers are the swap to avoid, because TG18 has its own organ thresholds.

say.text: Yes. TG18 scores the lungs on the PaO2/FiO2 ratio, and a value below 300 is a Grade III organ criterion.
The answer is the PaO2/FiO2 ratio below 300. TG18 grades the lungs by this ratio, and any one organ failure makes the grade III.
TG18 does not score the lungs on a raw oxygen level. It uses a ratio that takes into account how much oxygen the patient is being given.
Before you decide on ERCP, you want the bile duct mapped without passing any instrument into it. Which test do you choose?

choices.label: Diagnostic ERCP, with an endoscope and contrast
Contrast CT of the abdomen, portal venous phase
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: That is not the right choice.
ERCP is a good duct test, but it is invasive, and it is the treatment route once a stone is likely to need removing.
That is not the right choice.
CT is used for complications and for other diagnoses, and it misses many gallstones in the duct.
Yes. MRCP is the non-invasive investigation of choice for bile duct stones, with no instrument passed.
The answer is MRCP. It is the non-invasive test for CBD stones, while ERCP is both diagnostic and therapeutic and is kept for when a stone is likely.
Ask which option passes no instrument into the duct at all.
Forget the first test you order. Which investigation is the most sensitive and specific for acute cholecystitis itself?

choices.label: Ultrasonography, a bedside sound study of the gallbladder
HIDA (cholescintigraphy), a tracer uptake study of the gallbladder
Contrast CT of the abdomen and pelvis for the gallbladder
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: That is not the right choice.
Ultrasound is the initial test you order first, which is why it feels like the answer; it is not the test for most sensitive and specific.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check this one: the test you order first is not the test that answers 'most sensitive and specific'.

say.text: That is not the right choice.
CT is useful for complications such as perforation and abscess, but it misses many gallstones and is not the test for this question.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check this one: the test you order first is not the test that answers 'most sensitive and specific'.

say.text: Yes. A HIDA scan showing non-visualisation of the gallbladder, with tracer in the duodenum, is the most sensitive and specific test.
The answer is the HIDA scan. Non-filling of the gallbladder with tracer in the duodenum confirms cystic duct obstruction; ultrasound remains the first test.
Ask which test shows whether bile is entering the gallbladder, not just what the gallbladder looks like.
A PYQ key says acute cholecystitis is managed with conservative care, then interval surgery at 6 to 8 weeks. What do you write as current practice for a fit patient?

choices.label: Conservative care, then interval cholecystectomy at 6-8 weeks
Early laparoscopic cholecystectomy in the same admission
Antibiotics alone, with surgery only if symptoms recur
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: That is not the right choice.
The 6-8 week plan is the older PYQ key, built on letting the inflammation settle first, and it is not the current plan.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check this one: the older key and current practice differ here, and the key is what the PYQ expects.

say.text: That is not the right choice.
Antibiotics alone leave the diseased gallbladder in place, and waiting for recurrence was the older key's habit.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check this one: the older key and current practice differ here, and the key is what the PYQ expects.

say.text: Yes. Early laparoscopic cholecystectomy in the index admission, ideally within 72 hours, is current practice; the PYQ key expected interval surgery.
The answer is early laparoscopic cholecystectomy in the same admission, ideally within 72 hours of onset. The PYQ key expected conservative care then interval surgery.
The question asks for current practice, not the PYQ key. Ask what a fit patient gets during the index admission.
Which statement about treatment by TG18 grade is correct?

choices.label: Early laparoscopic surgery first in all three grades
Grade I, and fit Grade II, go to early laparoscopic surgery
Grade III goes straight to early laparoscopic surgery
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: That is not the right choice.
A single first step for every grade ignores that organ failure makes an operation unsafe at first.
That is not the right choice.
Grade III means organ failure, so the grade changes the first step before any operation.
Yes. Grade I goes to early laparoscopic cholecystectomy, and a fit Grade II can too; Grade III is supported and drained first.
The answer: Grade I, and a fit Grade II, go to early laparoscopic surgery; Grade III needs organ support and gallbladder drainage first.
Each grade has its own first step. Ask which grades tolerate early surgery, and which need the patient supported first.
A woman has gallstones on a scan done for a sore elbow. She has never had pain. She asks for tablets to dissolve the stones so she can avoid surgery. What do you tell her?

choices.label: Ursodeoxycholic acid tablets for six months, then review
Laparoscopic cholecystectomy now, as stones raise cancer risk
Reassure her; no treatment now, review if symptoms start

say.text: That is not the right choice.
Dissolution works only for small radiolucent cholesterol stones in a working gallbladder, so the stone type comes first.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check this one: a silent stone is not treated by default, and tablets need specific stone qualifiers.

say.text: That is not the right choice.
Stones are a risk, but the yearly chance of symptoms is low, so the size and symptoms of that risk come before surgery.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check this one: a silent stone is not treated by default, and tablets need specific stone qualifiers.

say.text: Yes. Most gallstones are silent, and symptoms develop at roughly 1 to 2 per cent a year, so expectant management is right.
The answer is reassurance and review. Most gallstones never cause symptoms, and prophylactic surgery is kept for selected high-risk cases.
Which sign is NOT part of Reynolds' pentad in acute cholangitis?
That is not the right choice.
Hypotension is not in the triad, but it is one of the two extra signs that turn the triad into the pentad.
That is not the right choice.
Confusion is not in the triad, but it is the second extra sign that makes up the pentad.
Yes. Charcot's triad is fever with rigors, jaundice and RUQ pain; hypotension and confusion make the pentad. Vomiting is in neither set.
The answer is vomiting. Charcot's triad plus hypotension and confusion makes Reynolds' pentad, and vomiting is in neither set.
A plain film shows gas in the gallbladder wall. Which statement about this finding is correct?

choices.label: E. coli, the commonest organism in infected bile, is the cause
Klebsiella, as in any infected gallbladder, is the cause
Gas-forming organisms, most often Clostridium perfringens, are the cause

say.text: That is not the right choice.
E. coli is the commonest organism in infected bile in general, but gas in the wall points to a different group of organisms.
That is not the right choice.
Klebsiella infects bile, but gas in the wall points to a gas-forming organism, so the general list does not apply.
Yes. Gas in the wall means emphysematous cholecystitis, caused by gas-forming organisms, most often Clostridium perfringens.
The answer is a gas-forming organism, most often Clostridium perfringens, classically in an elderly diabetic man. E. coli is the commonest organism in plain infected bile.
Day two after laparoscopic cholecystectomy, the drain shows green bile. What is the most likely cause?

choices.label: A blind clip across a bleeding vessel near the duct
Right hepatic artery injury in the triangle
Common bile duct mistaken for the cystic duct, then divided

say.text: That is not the right choice.
Bleeding is the dramatic complication, but it is not the commonest way the duct gets injured.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check this one: the most feared event is not the commonest cause of a duct injury.

say.text: That is not the right choice.
The hepatic artery sits near the duct, but injury to it is not the usual route to a major duct injury.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check this one: the most feared event is not the commonest cause of a duct injury.

say.text: Yes. Misidentifying the bile duct as the cystic duct is the commonest cause of major duct injury, which is why the view is confirmed before clipping.
The answer is misidentification of the bile duct as the cystic duct. That is the commonest cause of major duct injury, and the critical view prevents it.
Which three findings together make the critical view of safety, so that you can clip?

choices.label: Two structures seen; no need to clear the triangle
Cystic duct dissected alone down to the bile duct, then clipped
Triangle cleared; lower gallbladder off the liver bed; two structures only

say.text: That is not the right choice.
Seeing two structures is one of the three requirements, not the whole view, and the other two must also be met.
That is not the right choice.
Dissecting the cystic duct alone skips the triangle and the gallbladder's lower third, and that is what the view depends on.
Yes. The critical view needs the triangle cleared, the lower gallbladder off the liver bed, and only two structures seen.
The answer: the triangle is cleared, the lower gallbladder is separated from the liver bed, and only two structures are seen. All three are required.
Which patient with acalculous cholecystitis can have a laparoscopic cholecystectomy in the index admission?

choices.label: A ventilated patient on noradrenaline after a long laparotomy
A fit patient with no stone and no organ failure
A burns patient on day five in ICU, unfit for theatre

say.text: That is not the right choice.
A ventilated patient on vasopressors cannot tolerate a long operation, so the first step is drainage, not theatre.
That is not the right choice.
A burns patient in the ICU is at high risk from stasis and ischaemia, and the unfit patient is drained first.
Yes. Acalculous disease in a fit patient can be treated like calculous disease; unfit or critically ill patients are drained first.
The answer is a fit patient with no organ failure. Unfit or critically ill patients with acalculous disease are drained first, with percutaneous cholecystostomy.
Which pairing of syndrome and site is correct?

choices.label: Gallstone ileus, stone in the duodenum or pylorus
Bouveret's syndrome, stone in the duodenum or pylorus
Mirizzi syndrome, stone in the common bile duct lumen

say.text: That is not the right choice.
Gallstone ileus is small-bowel obstruction from a stone that has passed through a fistula, so it is not an outlet block at the duodenum.
That is not the right choice.
Mirizzi is a stone outside the duct pressing on the common hepatic duct, not a stone in the bile duct lumen.
Yes. Bouveret's syndrome is gastric outlet obstruction from a stone impacted in the duodenum or pylorus.
The answer is Bouveret's syndrome, with the stone in the duodenum or pylorus. Gallstone ileus obstructs the terminal ileum, and Mirizzi compresses the hepatic duct from outside.

cards.q: Most sensitive and specific test for acute cholecystitis?
cards.a: HIDA scan: non-visualisation of the gallbladder with tracer in the duodenum. Ultrasound is only the first test.

cards.q: Non-invasive investigation of choice for CBD stones?
cards.a: MRCP. ERCP is both diagnostic and therapeutic, so it is kept for when a stone is likely.
PaO2/FiO2 ratio below 300; any one organ dysfunction makes the grade III.

cards.q: Treatment of choice for acute calculous cholecystitis in a fit patient?
cards.a: Early laparoscopic cholecystectomy in the index admission, ideally within 72 hours.

cards.q: Asymptomatic gallstones: what is the default?
cards.a: Expectant management; symptoms develop at roughly 1 to 2 per cent a year.

cards.q: Where does gallstone ileus usually impact, and what is Rigler's triad?
cards.a: The terminal ileum. Rigler's triad: pneumobilia, small-bowel obstruction and an ectopic gallstone.

cards.q: Commonest cause of major bile duct injury?
cards.a: Misidentifying the common bile duct as the cystic duct; confirm the critical view before clipping.
